catalog_quote: 3.1.3 Word-internal metrical structure. A distinction between metrically strong and weak positions in words is mainly relevant to syncope/apocope and stress/accent. In Tigemaxo, syncope and apocope are limited to short high vowels {u i} preceded by a sonorant, especially {r l n}. ... Tigemaxo tone patterns have few similarities to those of pitch-accent languages. Lexical tone melodies mostly begin with nonlow tone and include /H/, /M/, /HLH/, /HM/, and /HL/, the latter with subtypes. ... The lexical melodies are subject to grammatical tone overlays, for example dropping /H/ to all-low. Both H-Terracing, which produces level tone terraces extending beyond individual words, and the more local M-Terracing, are important in prosodic phrasing. new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Tigemaxo has an empty rule; this grammar supplies the missing statement: tonal (three levels), no word-level accentual/stress system. It fills a blank rather than contradicting anything. Identity: describes the Dia-village dialect (Tigemaxo proper); Heath says Tigemaxo and Tiéyaxo are dialects of one language (p. 1) and that no general description of Tiéyaxo exists (p. 3).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tigemaxo (dialect of Dia) is a three-level (H/M/L) tone language with mora as tone-bearing unit; Heath states there is no weight-sensitive word-level accentual system, that the tone patterns are unlike pitch accent systems, and that foot structure has no analytical value. No word-stress placement rule exists or is given.
new_statements.exceptions: The locative yɛ̄ɛ̄ 'therein' is called 'an enclitic-like unstressed form' (p. 313), an informal use of 'unstressed' for a clitic; no stress system is implied.
new_statements.identity_note: Both listed 'Glottolog description' works are misfiled against tiey1235: Heath 2023 describes Kelenga (Hainyaxo), a distinct Bozo language (glottocode hain1238, Ké-Macina near Ségou), and Müller 2007 is a German syntax lecture handout. The directly relevant source is Heath 2025, A Grammar of Tigemaxo of Dia (Zenodo 15160216), which describes the Dia-village dialect of the Tigemaxo-Tiéyaxo language; Heath states 'Tigemaxo, described here, and Tiéyaxo are dialects of the same language' (p. 1) and that no general description of Tiéyaxo exists (p. 3), so the reading is for the Tigemaxo (Dia) dialect and is assumed to cover the cluster.

audit.reasoning: The 'tonal, no word-stress rule' coding rests on a 2025 open-access 674-page reference grammar by the language's principal modern describer, held held by the project with both deciding quotations verified verbatim at the stated pages (p.22 sec. 3.1.3; p.39 sec. 3.5). The author explicitly denies a weight-sensitive word-level accentual system and any role for foot structure, and describes a three-level H/M/L tone system with lexical melodies and grammatical overlays. The only older grammar in Glottolog (Blecke 1996) excludes phonology by the author's own statement as reported by Heath; the remaining Glottolog items are either mis-tagged syntax textbooks, a grammar of a sister language, or pre-tonology orthography/morphology works. sources.note: Only dedicated phonology article touching Tigemaxo tone; downloaded now, confirms the three-level tonal analysis and is silent on stress. No other unheld work would improve this record: Blecke 1996 (Glottolog's top grammar) explicitly excludes phonology per Heath 2025 p.8.

sources.note: Describes Kelenga (Hainyaxo), glottocode hain1238, a distinct Bozo language spoken near Ké-Macina; Glottolog attached it to tiey1235 apparently because of the 'Hainyaxo' name. Heath's own classification in this grammar (p. 1) lists 'Tigemaxo and Tiéyaxo' and 'Kelenga (= Hainyaxo)' as separate Bozo languages. Its no-stress statement is about Kelenga, not Tigemaxo, though it is compatible with what Heath 2025 says about Tigemaxo.
